• Range is the maximum geographic distance consumers are willing to travel to purchase a good or service. Threshold is the minimum population or purchasing market size required to sustain a business and operate profitably.
Part B: Explain Range Disparity Using Data (2 pts):
• Establishment 1 Short Range (1 pt): A convenience store sells inexpensive everyday staples (milk, snacks) that are widely available; consumers will not travel more than 1 to 2 miles because travel cost exceeds the item's value.
• Establishment 3 Long Range (1 pt): A pediatric cancer hospital provides rare, highly specialized medical treatments unavailable locally; because the service is critical and unique, patients and families are willing to travel 60 to 90+ miles to access specialized care.
Part C: Why Hexagons Instead of Circles (2 pts):
• Explanation (2 pts): Circular market areas leave either unserved geometric gaps where consumers have no access to central goods, or overlapping areas where adjacent centers engage in contested market competition. Regular hexagons are the geometric shape closest to circles that tile a flat plain completely without gaps or overlaps while minimizing average travel distance from the boundary to the central place.
Part D: Nesting Hierarchy of Settlements (2 pts):
• Description (2 pts): At the base of the urban hierarchy, small settlements (hamlets and villages) providing basic low-order goods are numerous and closely spaced together. As one ascends the hierarchy to towns and large cities, settlements become progressively fewer in number, are spaced much further apart, and provide specialized high-order services in addition to all the low-order services found in smaller settlements.
Part E: Modern E-Commerce Alteration of Range (2 pts):
• Explanation (2 pts): Online retail platforms (e.g., Amazon) and home parcel delivery allow rural consumers to purchase specialized high-order goods (niche electronics, specialized books) directly from home without traveling physical distances, effectively expanding the consumer's access to an infinite digital range while rendering physical central place proximity obsolete for non-perishable goods.

Part C: Inversion of North American Burgess Wealth Gradient (2 pts):

In the Griffin-Ford Latin American model, this gradient is completely inverted: the wealthiest elites occupy the central core and paved spine, while socioeconomic status declines outward, culminating in impoverished squatter settlements on the outer periphery.
Part D: Physical and Municipal Conditions of Disamenity Sector (2 pts):
• Description (2 pts): Disamenity sectors are located on dangerous, undesirable physical terrain (such as steep mountain ravines prone to catastrophic mudslides, or polluted industrial river floodplains). They lack basic municipal water, sewer, and electrical grids, and frequently operate outside formal police control, dominated by informal community leaders or drug cartels.
Part E: Influence of Spanish Laws of the Indies (2 pts):
• Explanation (2 pts): Enacted in 1573, the Laws of the Indies were royal urban planning regulations issued by the Spanish Crown that required colonial settlements to follow a standardized geometric gridiron street pattern centered on a rectangular central plaza (plaza mayor). The Catholic cathedral, governor's palace, and elite residences were mandated to border the plaza, embedding colonial religious and administrative authority at the spatial heart of the city.

Without formal legal land deeds to serve as collateral, commercial banks refuse to grant women business loans or agricultural credit, enforcing economic dependence on male relatives.

Part Scoring Criteria & Benchmark Expectation Points
Part A Accurately defines GII scale: 0 = equality, 1 = maximum inequality. 1
Part B Explains how high adolescent birth rates and maternal mortality truncate education and formal employment. 2
Part C Explains how education and career entry lower TFR below replacement. 2
Part D Describes small collateral-free microloans enabling independent business generation. 2
Part E Describes a valid institutional barrier (customary land tenure denial, lack of credit access). 2

FRQ SCORING GUIDELINES QUESTION 247 OF 250 • UNIT 7: INDUSTRIAL AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT PATTERNS AND PROCESSES

Theories of Development: Modernization vs. World Systems Theory

9 Points Total
OFFICIAL AP MODEL RESPONSE:
PARTA:
• Stage 3: Takeoff.
PARTB:
• Rostow's model is criticized for being Eurocentric and ahistorical: it assumes every country can replicate the Western European experience in isolation, ignoring how historical colonialism depleted peripheral natural resources and erected structural trade barriers that lock developing nations into dependent primary commodity extraction.
PARTC:
• Core nations (e.g., the US, Japan, Germany) exploit the periphery by extracting cheap raw materials, agricultural crops, and low-wage manual labor. Core countries process these inputs into high-value manufactured goods and high-tech quaternary services, exporting them back at high profit while dominating global banking, enforcing an unequal flow of capital.
PARTD:
• Brazil (or China, Mexico, India) is semi-peripheral because it exhibits a dual economic structure: it contains advanced manufacturing centers (automobiles, aerospace, steel) and growing urban tech hubs, but also large impoverished rural populations engaged in primary resource extraction (soy, iron ore, cattle) while remaining partially dependent on core investment capital.
PARTE:
• Sub-nationally, economic core-periphery dynamics appear within borders: for example, in Italy, the northern industrial triangle (Milan, Turin, Genoa) functions as a high-income, technological core, while the southern Mezzogiorno functions as an agrarian periphery characterized by lower incomes, out-migration, and structural underdevelopment.
OFFICIAL AP SCORING RUBRIC (9 POINTS BREAKDOWN):
Part Scoring Criteria & Benchmark Expectation Points
Part A Identifies Stage 3 (Takeoff). 1
Part B Explains Eurocentrism and neglect of colonial legacy/dependency. 2
Part C Explains unequal exchange: raw extraction/cheap labor from periphery vs high-tech/financial dominance in core. 2
Part D Identifies a valid semi-periphery state and explains its dual industrial/extractive profile. 2
Part E Applies core-periphery to an internal regional divide (e.g., North vs South Italy). 2

FRQ SCORING GUIDELINES QUESTION 248 OF 250 • UNIT 7: INDUSTRIAL AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT PATTERNS AND PROCESSES

Commodity Dependence, Export Vulnerability, and Global Terms of Trade

9 Points Total
OFFICIAL AP MODEL RESPONSE:
PARTA:
• A country is classified as commodity-dependent when primary commodities (agricultural crops, timber, minerals, fossil fuels) account for 60% or more of its total merchandise export earnings.
PARTB:
• Because Angola (93% oil) and Zambia (77% copper) rely almost entirely on single commodities for their foreign exchange and corporate tax receipts, a global market price crash immediately hollows out government revenues, leaving them unable to service sovereign debts, pay public employees, or fund healthcare.
PARTC:
• Under the Prebisch-Singer thesis, over the long term, the prices of raw primary commodities decline relative to the prices of sophisticated manufactured goods produced in core nations. Consequently, a commodity-exporting country must export ever-larger volumes of cocoa, oil, or copper simply to import the same quantity of manufactured machinery, tractors, or pharmaceuticals.
PARTD:
• Dutch Disease occurs when a massive boom in resource exports (e.g., oil) causes huge foreign currency inflows, sharply appreciating the domestic exchange rate. This overvalued currency makes the country's other export sectors (such as domestic manufacturing and farming) uncompetitively expensive abroad while making foreign imports cheaper, causing domestic industrial factories to shutter.
PARTE:
• The government can mandate and subsidize 'value-added beneficiation'—processing raw materials domestically (e.g., refining cocoa beans into chocolate, smelting copper into electrical wiring) before export, creating secondary industrial jobs and shielding the economy from raw price volatility.
OFFICIAL AP SCORING RUBRIC (9 POINTS BREAKDOWN):
Part Scoring Criteria & Benchmark Expectation Points
Part A Identifies the UNCTAD threshold: primary commodities >= 60% of merchandise exports. 1
Part B Explains single-commodity vulnerability causing fiscal revenue collapse using table data. 2
Part C Explains declining terms of trade (raw prices fall relative to manufactured imports). 2
Part D Defines Dutch Disease and currency appreciation undermining domestic manufacturing. 2
Part E Describes a valid diversification strategy (value-added processing, sovereign wealth fund). 2

FRQ SCORING GUIDELINES QUESTION 249 OF 250 • UNIT 7: INDUSTRIAL AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT PATTERNS AND PROCESSES

Supranational Trade Blocs, Tariffs, and Neoliberal Trade Policies

9 Points Total
OFFICIAL AP MODEL RESPONSE:
PARTA:
• A tariff is a government-imposed customs tax levied on foreign imported goods at the national border, designed to increase import prices and generate revenue.
PARTB:
• Comparative advantage states that countries maximize overall economic output when they specialize in producing goods where their opportunity cost is lowest, trading for goods produced more efficiently by partners. Dismantling tariffs within USMCA allows each nation to specialize (e.g., US in capital-intensive design/quaternary tech, Mexico in labor-intensive assembly), lowering consumer prices across the trade bloc.
PARTC:
• The elimination of tariffs incentivized multinational automotive and appliance firms to shift labor-intensive assembly plants south of the border into Mexico's northern maquiladora corridor, taking advantage of lower Mexican wages while re-exporting finished components duty-free into the US market.
PARTD:
• Labor unions argue that free trade agreements facilitate 'social dumping'—corporations offshore well-paying, unionized domestic manufacturing jobs to developing nations with weaker environmental regulations and lower wages, leading to plant closures, wage stagnation, and localized deindustrialization in domestic industrial belts.
PARTE:
• Because modern manufacturing relies on synchronized 'just-in-time' logistics with minimal inventory stockpiles, a blockage at a single maritime bottleneck (like the Suez Canal) halts thousands of shipping containers. Within days, manufacturing plants thousands of miles away run out of critical parts and are forced to idle production lines, revealing extreme spatial fragility.
OFFICIAL AP SCORING RUBRIC (9 POINTS BREAKDOWN):
Part Scoring Criteria & Benchmark Expectation Points
Part A Accurately defines a tariff as a tax on imported goods. 1
Part B Explains comparative advantage (lower opportunity cost specialization) justifying tariff elimination. 2
Part C Explains spatial relocation of assembly to Mexican maquiladoras under USMCA. 2
Part D Describes a valid labor critique (offshoring, plant closures, wage pressure). 2
Part E Explains supply chain interdependence and just-in-time vulnerability. 2

FRQ SCORING GUIDELINES QUESTION 250 OF 250 • UNIT 7: INDUSTRIAL AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT PATTERNS AND PROCESSES

Deindustrialization, Rust Belt Landscapes, and Sunbelt Growth Poles

9 Points Total
OFFICIAL AP MODEL RESPONSE:
PARTA:
• Deindustrialization is the sustained structural contraction and decline of industrial manufacturing activity and employment within a region or country, accompanied by a transition toward a service-oriented economy.
PARTB:
• First, technological automation replaced thousands of assembly-line workers with industrial robotics, dramatically reducing labor requirements per manufactured vehicle or ton of steel. Second, corporate globalization and trade liberalization led firms to offshore labor-intensive production to lower-wage facilities in the US South, Mexico, and East Asia to reduce operating costs.
PARTC:
• A brownfield is an abandoned, derelict, or underused industrial site whose redevelopment is complicated by hazardous environmental contamination. Pittsburgh successfully repurposed former blast-furnace sites along its rivers into mixed-use commercial districts, medical research facilities, robotics laboratories, and urban green spaces.
PARTD:
• First, Texas offers a pro-business regulatory environment featuring no state personal income tax, lower corporate taxes, and non-unionized labor markets. Second, Austin is anchored by a premier research institution (University of Texas at Austin) that produces an abundant talent pool of skilled software and electrical engineers, complemented by warm weather and cultural lifestyle amenities.
PARTE:
• The multiplier effect occurs when new basic quaternary tech jobs bring external wealth into the region, which is spent locally, stimulating non-basic tertiary employment: each new software engineering position generates 3 to 5 additional jobs in construction, restaurants, healthcare, retail, and local schools.

APPENDIX COMPREHENSIVE SPATIAL MODELS & THEORIES MATRIX

Comprehensive Spatial Models & Theories Reference

Quick Reference Matrix of Foundational Geographic Models across Units 1 through 7 for the AP Human Geography Examination.

1. Population & Migration Models

  • Demographic Transition Model (DTM): Stages 1–5 tracking CBR, CDR, and NIR as societies industrialize.
  • Epidemiologic Transition Model: Pestilence/famine → receding pandemics → degenerative diseases → delayed degenerative.
  • Ravenstein's Laws of Migration: Most migrants move short distances, to big cities, are young adults, and adult males dominate international moves.

2. Agricultural & Rural Land-Use Models

  • Von Thünen Model (1826): Concentric rings based on bid-rent and transportation costs: 1) Market gardening & dairying, 2) Forest/wood, 3) Extensive grain/field crops, 4) Ranching/livestock grazing.
  • Cadastral Systems: Metes & bounds (irregular physical landmarks), Township & range (uniform 6×6 mile grids), Long-lot (river access ribbons).

3. Urban Land-Use & Hierarchy Models

  • Christaller's Central Place Theory: Hexagonal hinterlands, range (max travel distance), threshold (min population needed).
  • Burgess Concentric Zone (1925): 5 concentric rings radiating from CBD; Zone of Transition.
  • Hoyt Sector Model (1939): Directional wedges along rail/transit corridors.
  • Harris-Ullman Multiple Nuclei (1945): Polycentric nodes; auto-oriented.
  • Galactic / Peripheral Model: Beltway ring roads, edge cities, suburban office nodes.

4. Industrial, Economic & Political Models

  • Weber's Least Cost Theory (1909): Transport cost minimization; bulk-reducing (material-oriented) vs. bulk-gaining (market-oriented).
  • Rostow's Modernization (1960): 5 linear stages: Traditional → Preconditions → Takeoff → Drive to Maturity → High Mass Consumption.
  • Wallerstein's World Systems (1974): Global capitalist core, semi-periphery, and periphery division of labor and dependency.
  • Mackinder Heartland vs. Spykman Rimland: Eurasian geopolitical power theories.
Key Core Geographic Concepts:
• Possibilism: Physical environment sets limits, but human culture possesses the agency to adapt and innovate.
• Space-Time Compression: Technological reduction in time required for movement of goods, information, and people across space.
